value: after a virtual magnetic displacement 1,000 km east, sham-sectioned controls re-oriented (mean heading 323 deg, n 27) but birds with both ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal branches cut did not (mean heading 34 deg, n 22; headings differed between groups, P 0.022; lesioned birds' heading did not differ from their pre-surgery heading)
eye: not the eye; trigeminal-dependent magnetic positioning (map) sense, receptor not identified
method: behavioural: orientation in modified Emlen funnels in a four-coil system simulating the field of a site 1,000 km east, after bilateral sectioning of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve versus sham operation
conditions: Wild-caught migrants, 49 birds (22 sectioned, 27 sham); tests are of map (position) information, not of the compass; the control and lesioned birds were each oriented only weakly (r 0.39 in both groups); the authors link the lesioned birds' failure to the same failure after a real physical displacement; spring migration, tested in May 2013 to 2015 and 2017; groups compared by Mardia-Watson-Wheeler test (W 7.66); sham birds' heading shifted from pre-surgery 48 deg (P 0.004)

quote: Birds with bilaterally ablated ophthalmic branches of the trigeminal nerves were not able to re-orient towards their conspecific breeding grounds after a virtual magnetic displacement, exactly like they were not able to compensate for a real physical displacement.
note: Species is the Eurasian reed warbler. Not on main for this species and trait (grep by taxon and DOI). value: with a small neodymium magnet on the forehead and only the magnetic field available, birds were randomly oriented (r 0.17, P 0.70, n 12), whereas untreated birds headed south-east (mean 147 deg, r 0.47, P 0.02, n 17)
eye: not the eye; magnetic compass, receptor not identified
method: behavioural: orientation in modified Emlen funnels, control (no attachment), magnet and sham treatments
conditions: Experiment 1 (12 September to 4 October 2019): 17 first-year birds caught at Lake Neusiedl in early September, each tested under control, magnet and sham treatments (four tests each); funnels outdoors under a translucent lid blocking the sky, so no celestial cues; disc magnets 3 mm by 2 mm, 0.11 g, raising local total intensity by about 83,000 nT at 2 cm above the pole against about 48,800 nT of the Earth's field; magnet-group sample 12 of the 17 birds; sham birds oriented (167 deg, r 0.65, P 0.002, n 14), not different from controls

where: Results, Experiment 1 (journal PDF; sentence read on two fetches)
quote: During magnet tests, the birds were randomly oriented (Rayleigh test: r=0.17, P=0.70, n=12; Fig. 4A) and their circular distribution was best described by the uniform orientation model (Table 1).
note: Disrupted orientation by a magnet is an indirect test of the magnetic compass. Licence: Crossref lists CC BY 4.0 and the journal PDF states the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0). value: with magnets on the forehead and celestial cues available, birds were oriented south-east (mean 146 deg, r 0.51, P 0.01, n 16); with magnets and no celestial cues they were not oriented unimodally (r 0.23, P 0.48, n 15; best fit a symmetric bimodal model, uniform model close)
eye: not the eye; magnetic compass, receptor not identified
method: behavioural: orientation in modified Emlen funnels with magnets attached, with and without access to stars
conditions: Experiment 2 (10 to 22 September 2020), 18 first-year birds caught at Lake Neusiedl in September; every Experiment 2 condition carried a magnet (no magnet-free control in 2020) and magnet polarity was reversed relative to Experiment 1, so the masking reading compares this cohort with the 2019 cohort's control and magnet results; the authors read the restored orientation as birds falling back on another compass system, so the test does not isolate magnetic input once celestial cues exist

value: two lizards learned to discriminate light from dark blue, one rewarded for light blue (criterion after 6 sessions) and one for dark blue (criterion after 10 sessions); pilot only, descriptive
method: behavioural: operant two-choice discrimination, lizards touch the cue card carrying the rewarded colour
conditions: Pilot with 2 wild-caught adults (Fowlers Gap, New South Wales, caught March 2018), one target training plus nine discrimination trials per day, criterion 8 of 9 correct in each of two consecutive sessions after at least three sessions; no statistics; one lizard (ID8) assigned light blue and the other (ID9) dark blue as correct; pilot April to June 2019; both lizards then failed the reversal (0 correct choices and no choice); only light against dark blue was tested, so this does not show hue discrimination

value: none of six naive lizards reached the learning criterion for two squares against eight squares in the first 11 sessions
method: behavioural: operant two-choice discrimination of grey cards bearing two or eight black squares (10 by 10 mm each)
conditions: Six naive wild-caught adults, three rewarded for the two-square card and three for the eight-square card; criterion 8 of 9 correct in each of two consecutive sessions; after five procedural changes two of six (both rewarded for eight squares) reached criterion at sessions 53 and 54; the authors attribute the difficulty mainly to the shared middle squares prompting generalisation, set aside low acuity, and hypothesise handling stress, so the first 11 sessions are not a measure of the lizards' limit
